title: Actinidia arguta
wikitext:
{{short description|Species of plant}} {{Speciesbox |name = Hardy kiwi |image = Weiki01.jpg |genus = Actinidia |species = arguta |authority = ([[Philipp Franz von Siebold|Siebold]] & [[Zucc.]]) [[Planch.]] ex [[Miq.]] }} '''''Actinidia arguta''''' is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[vine]] native to Japan, [[Korea]], Northern China, and the [[Russian Far East]]. The fruit is known as '''kiwiberry''' or '''hardy kiwi''',{{Cite web |title=Choosing kiwiberry varieties {{!}} Minnesota Fruit Research |url=https://fruit.umn.edu/news/choosing-kiwiberry-varieties |access-date=2024-10-16 |website=fruit.umn.edu}} which are small [[kiwifruit]]s without the hair-like fiber covering the outside, unlike most other species of the genus.{{cite web |url=http://www.crfg.org/pubs/ff/hardy-kiwifruit.html |title=Hardy Kiwifruit |date=1996 |publisher=California Rare Fruit Growers, Inc. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110410192244/http://www.crfg.org/pubs/ff/hardy-kiwifruit.html |archive-date=2011-04-10}} == Description == The fruit is referred to as the kiwiberry, arctic kiwi, baby kiwi, cocktail kiwi, dessert kiwi, grape kiwi, hardy kiwifruit, northern kiwi, Siberian gooseberry, or Siberian kiwi, with the name kiwiberry gaining in popularity in the 2010s and 2020s.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|pp=37}} It is an edible, berry- or grape-sized fruit similar to [[kiwifruit]] in taste and appearance, but is green, brownish, or purple with smooth skin, sometimes with a red blush. Often sweeter and sharper-tasting than the kiwifruit, hardy kiwifruit can be eaten whole and do not need to be peeled. Thin-walled, its exterior is smooth and leathery.{{Cite web |title=Actinidia arguta (Bower actinidia, Bower Vine, Chamdarae, Cocktail Kiwi, Darae, Dessert Kiwi, Hardy Kiwi, Hardy Kiwi Vine, Kokuwa, Sarunashi, Siberian Gooseberry, Tarae, Tara Vine, Yang-tao) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/actinidia-arguta/ |access-date=2023-07-17 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}} File:Hardy-Kiwi-Comparison-3.jpg|The larger kiwifruit in back compared to the smaller size of the hardy kiwi in front File:Actinidia-arguta-foliage.jpg|Leaves File:Actinidia-arguta-flowers.jpg|Flowers File:Kiwiberry cross section.jpg|Fruits == Botanical history and taxonomy == [[File:Actinidia hypoleuca - Miyajima Natural Botanical Garden - DSC02388.JPG|thumb|''Actinidia arguta'' var. ''hypoleuca'']] ''Actinidia arguta'' was first described by [[Philipp Franz von Siebold]] and [[Joseph Gerhard Zuccarini]] in 1843 as ''Trochostigma argutum''.{{GRIN|id=40670|name=''Trochostigma argutum'' Siebold & Zucc.|accessdate=26 March 2010}} It was then moved to the genus ''Actinidia'' in 1867 by [[Friedrich Anton Wilhelm Miquel]] after the invalidly published suggestion by [[Jules Émile Planchon]] to move the species.{{GRIN|id=1389|name=''Actinidia arguta'' (Siebold & Zucc.) Planch. ex Miq.|accessdate=26 March 2010}} === Varieties === The species consists of three [[variety (botany)|varieties]]:{{cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:316460-1 |title=Actinidia arguta (Siebold & Zucc.) Planch. ex Miq. |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=6 May 2025}} *''Actinidia arguta'' var. ''arguta'' ([[autonym (botany)|autonym]]) *''Actinidia arguta'' var. ''giraldii'' ([[Ludwig Diels|Diels]]) [[Vorosch.]] *''Actinidia arguta'' var. ''hypoleuca'' ([[Takenoshin Nakai|Nakai]]) [[Kitam.]] ''Actinidia arguta'' var. ''giraldii'' was originally described by [[Ludwig Diels]] at the species rank (''Actinidia giraldii'') in 1905,{{GRIN|id=419962|name=''Actinidia giraldii'' Diels|accessdate=26 March 2010}} but was later reduced to a variety of ''A. arguta'' in 1972 by [[Vladimir Nikolaevich Voroschilov]].{{GRIN|id=419961|name=''Actinidia arguta'' (Siebold & Zucc.) Planch. ex Miq. var. ''giraldii'' (Diels) Vorosch.|accessdate=26 March 2010}} ''A. arguta'' var. ''hypoleuca'' was originally described at the species rank (''Actinidia hypoleuca'') by [[Takenoshin Nakai]] in 1904,{{GRIN|id=420050|name=''Actinidia hypoleuca'' Nakai|accessdate=26 March 2010}} but reduced to a variety of ''A. arguta'' in 1980 by [[Siro Kitamura]].{{GRIN|id=459544|name=''Actinidia arguta'' (Siebold & Zucc.) Planch. ex Miq. var. ''hypoleuca'' (Nakai) Kitam.|accessdate=26 March 2010}} In 2007, ''Actinidia purpurea'', the red hardy kiwi, was synonymised with ''Actinidia arguta'' var. ''arguta''.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|pp=41-42}} ''Actinidia arguta'' had been placed in [[section (botany)|section]] ''Leiocarpae'' and [[series (botany)|series]] ''Lamellatae'', but this current infrageneric classification is unsupported. A 2002 study of the nuclear DNA [[internal transcribed spacer]] sequence and the [[plastid]] ''matK'' gene sequence for [[cladistics|cladistic analysis]] revealed the current circumscription of the sections to be [[polyphyletic]], with ''A. arguta'' forming a [[clade]] with ''[[Actinidia melanandra|A. melanandra]]'' near the base of the [[phylogenetics|phylogenetic]] tree.{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Jianqiang |last2=Huang |first2=Hongwen |last3=Sang |first3=Tao |title=Molecular phylogeny and infrageneric classification of ''Actinidia'' (Actinidiaceae) |journal=Systematic Botany |date=2002 |volume=27 |issue=2 |pages=408–415 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3093880 |jstor=3093880 }} === Cultivars === [[File:Actinidia arguta 'Ken's Red' Aktinidia ostrolistna 2017-10-15 01.jpg|thumb|'Ken's Red', a hybrid cultivar of ''Actinidia arguta'' and ''[[Actinidia melanandra]]'']] Unlike kiwifruit, as of 2021 no single cultivar has been established as the predominant commercial cultivar.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|p=85}} The most popular cultivars in China include 'Long Cheng No. 2', 'LD133', 'Kuilv', and 'Chang Jiang No. 1', while 'Ananasnaya' (syn. 'Jumbo Verde') is the most commonly grown cultivar in the United States and Chile.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|pp=87-88}} In Europe, the most popular cultivars include 'Weiki', 'Geneva', and two proprietary cultivars from New Zealand, 'Hortgem Tahi' and 'Hortgem Rua'.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|pp=87-88}} Other cultivars include 'MSU', 'Super Jumbo', 'Rogow', 'Kievskaya Krupnoplodnaya', 'Taezhniy Dar' and 'Estafeta'. A commonly sold self-fertile hybrid is the Japanese cultivar 'Issai' (''A. arguta'' × ''polygama'') and its offspring 'Super Issai', while the hybrid 'Ken's Red' (''A. arguta'' × ''melanandra'') originates from New Zealand.{{cite journal |last1=Start |first1=MA |last2=Luby |first2=J |last3=Filler |first3=D |last4=Riera-Lizarazu |first4=O |last5=Guthrie |first5=R |title=Ploidy Levels of Cold-Hardy Actinidia Accessions in the United States Determined by Flow Cytometry |journal=Acta Hortic. |date=2007 |volume=753 |issue=753 |pages=161–168 |doi=10.17660/ActaHortic.2007.753.17 |url=https://www.ishs.org/ishs-article/753_17|url-access=subscription }} == Distribution and habitat == ''Actinidia arguta'' has one of the widest ranges of species within ''Actinidia'', found across China, eastern Russia, Korea, Taiwan and Japan. The plant is found in significantly colder areas compared to most other ''Actinidia'', typically between {{cvt|150-1500|m}} above sea level, including areas such as the [[Yan Mountains]] and northeastern Chinese provinces incluving [[Jilin]] and [[Liaoning]]. In southern Japan, the plant can grow at altitudes up to {{cvt|1900|m}} above sea level,{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|p=42}} and the plant has been recorded growing up to heights of {{cvt|3000|m}}.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|p=85}} The greatest number of wild records of ''Actinidia arguta'' come from central China, northeastern China, the Korean peninsula and Japan.{{Cite journal| volume = 29| issue = 2| pages = 1889| last1 = Wang| first1 = RL| last2 = Jiang| first2 = Chunxian| last3 = Huang| first3 = Tingting| last4 = Zhang| first4 = Zhe| last5 = Wang| first5 = Mingtiang| last6 = Shen| first6 = Zhanhong| last7 = Wang| first7 = Yanli| last8 = Li| first8 = Qing| title = A simulation study of the geographical distribution of Actinidia arguta in China| journal = Polish Journal of Environmental Studies| date = 2020| doi = 10.15244/pjoes/109306| bibcode = 2020PJES...29.1889W| doi-access = free}} The plants can grow in both mountainous and forested areas, and can survive winter temperatures of {{cvt|−45|°C}}, and summer temperatures exceeding {{cvt|37|°C}}.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|p=42}} [[Macrofossil]]s of ''A. arguta'' from the early [[Pliocene]] epoch have been found in western [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] in the [[Caucasus]] region.The History of the Flora and Vegetation of Georgia by Irina Shatilova, Nino Mchedlishvili, Luara Rukhadze, Eliso Kvavadze, [[Georgian National Museum]] Institute of [[Paleobiology]], [[Tbilisi]] 2011, {{ISBN|978-9941-9105-3-1}} == Cultivation history == ''Actinidia arguta'' was first cultivated in Europe and North America in the late 19th century as an ornamental plant.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|pp=40-41}} Some of the earliest seeds for European plantings were collected from [[Hokkaido]], Japan, by [[William S. Clark]] in 1876.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|pp=84-85}} The first commercial kiwiberry plantings were established in [[Oregon]], United States, in the late 1990s. This was followed by small plantings in New Zealand, Chile, Italy, France, and Switzerland.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|pp=40-41}} Attempts to commercialize the fruit have been historically unsuccessful due to its short shelf-life and sporadic tendencies to ripen. However, attempts are being made to bring the fruit to greater bear, and commercial production initiatives are underway on a small scale in [[South America]], New Zealand, Europe, Canada, and the United States (in [[Oregon]], [[Washington (U.S. state)|Washington]], and central [[Pennsylvania]]).[http://www.kiwiberry.com/kiwi%20korners.htm Kiwi Korners Farm], Commercial Production of Actinidia Arguta (Hardy Kiwi) South Korea's National Institute of Forest Science({{lang|ko|국립산림과학원}}) develops and distributes new hardy kiwi [[cultivar|cultivars]] as a high-value crop.{{Cite web |title=신품종 토종다래의 모든 것, 현장에서 직접 알려드립니다! - 보도자료 {{!}} 브리핑룸 {{!}} 대한민국 정책브리핑 |url=https://m.korea.kr/briefing/pressReleaseView.do?newsId=156155821#pressRelease |access-date=2025-05-03 |website=m.korea.kr}} Relative ease of maintenance of the trees due to low height is seen as an advantage as a commercial crop.{{Cite web |title=산림과수 블루오션을 향한 첫걸음! 다래, 신품종 현장설명회 개최 |url=https://go.seoul.co.kr/news/prnewsView.php?id=366599§ion=b_sec_1&page=147 |access-date=2025-05-03 |website=서울Pn}} The estimated total cultivation area for kiwiberry plantations in 2015 is {{cvt|1640|ha}}, of which {{cvt|1260|ha}} was found in China.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|pp=40-41}} Between 2015 and 2019, an additional {{cvt|2300|ha}} of kiwiberry plantations were established in China.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|pp=40-41}} As of 2023, {{cvt|45.4|t}} of kiwiberries were produced in South Korea, of which [[Gangwon Province, South Korea|Gangwon Province]] accounted for around {{cvt|30|t}}.{{Cite web |last=산림청 |year=2024 |orig-date=2024-11-26 |title=시도・소속기관별 임산물 생산현황 |url=https://kosis.kr/statHtml/statHtml.do?orgId=136&tblId=DT_136006_10878&conn_path=I2 |access-date=2025-05-03 |website=Korean Statistical Information Service |publisher=[[Statistics Korea]] |language=ko}} === Kazura bridges === [[File:Iya waddle bridge(Kazurabashi) 01.jpg|thumb|Iya Kazura Bridge in [[Miyoshi, Tokushima]], constructed using ''Actinidia arguta'' vines]] Kazura bridges ({{lang|ja|かずら橋}}) in [[Miyoshi, Tokushima]], Japan are a [[suspension bridge]]s made from ''Actinidia arguta'' vines.{{cite web|url=https://marushin-magazine.com/tokushima/iya-no-kazurabashi-sightseeing/ |title=大自然を楽しむ！「祖谷のかずら橋（徳島県）」の完全ガイド｜観光スポット（見所）・お土産・ホテル |website=M-Magazine |language=Japanese |date=19 September 2024 |access-date=6 May 2025}} Legends suggest the first bridges were made by [[Kūkai]] or fugitives of the [[Taira clan|Heike clan]], who could quickly cut the bridges if being pursued by people.{{cite web|url=https://www.miyoshi.i-tokushima.jp/fs/2/7/2/9/2/_/20_2.pdf |title=祖谷のかずら橋 − 三好市西祖谷山村善徳 − |author=市報みよし |website=City of Miyoshi |date=10 May 2006 |access-date=6 May 2025}} Documents from the mid-17th century record between seven and thirteen kazura bridges in the Iya valley. The most famous bridge is Iya Kazura Bridge ({{lang|ja|祖谷のかずら橋}}), which is {{cvt|45|m}} in length and crosses the Iya River. Likely recorded in 1815, the Iya Kazura Bridge was entirely made from vines until it was replaced by a wire suspension bridge in the 1920s, in order for carts and vehicles to be able to cross the river. The vine bridge was rebuilt in 1928, fortified with steel wire for the safety of tourists.{{cite journal|url=https://www.jcca.or.jp/kaishi/262/262_toku5.pdf |title=Enjoying the thrill "Kazura Vine Bridge in Iya" |last=Sokei |first=Hiroyuki |journal=Civil Engineering Consultant |volume=262 |date=January 2014 |access-date=6 May 2025 |pages=24–27}} The vines of the bridge need to be replaced every three years. Another kazura bridge was constructed in 1989 in [[Ikeda, Fukui]], as a tourist attraction imitating the originals in Tokushima Prefecture.{{cite web|url=http://www.asahi.com/travel/bridge/TKY201007220267.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100725022754/http://www.asahi.com/travel/bridge/TKY201007220267.html |archive-date=25 July 2010 |date=23 July 2010 |title=本家・徳島直伝、スリル満点 かずら橋（福井県）|website=The Asahi Shimbun |access-date=6 May 2025}} === Invasiveness in the United States === By the 2010s, vines of unknown genotype and provenance were reported by groups including Mass Audubon to be invasive in the United States, where ''Actinidia arguta'' vines have been seen to have rampant overgrowth and "complete domination of mature trees" at sites in western Massachusetts and Coffin Woods and North Shore Wildlife Sanctuary in Long Island, New York.{{cite web|url=http://www.massaudubon.org/learn/nature-wildlife/invasive-plants/hardy-kiwi|title=Hardy kiwi|publisher=Mass Audubon|date=2019|accessdate=30 April 2019}} Whether such localized sites indicate an [[invasive species|invasive risk]] for the region as a whole is controversial, given the long history of this widely distributed and cultivated species in the northeastern United States.Penn State Extension - Fruit Times. March 22, 2013. [http://extension.psu.edu/fruit-production/news/2013/hardy-kiwifruit-invasive-plant-or-throwback-to-the-gilded-age Hardy Kiwifruit: Invasive Plant or Throwback to the Gilded Age?] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130407035259/http://extension.psu.edu/fruit-production/news/2013/hardy-kiwifruit-invasive-plant-or-throwback-to-the-gilded-age |date=2013-04-07 }} Since successful invasions of non-native species can occur gradually over time, these reported sites warrant further investigation and suggest the need for more widespread monitoring.{{cite web|url=http://www.fws.gov/asheville/pdfs/Introductionandbackgroundmaterial.pdf |title=Exotic Invasive Plants of Southern Appalachia: An Activity Guide - introduction |accessdate=2013-03-27 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090512115037/http://www.fws.gov/asheville/pdfs/Introductionandbackgroundmaterial.pdf |archivedate=2009-05-12 }} == Cultivation techniques == [[File:Actinidia-arguta-habit.jpg|thumb|Cultivated vine trained on a [[trellis (architecture)|trellis]]]] The fast-growing, climbing, [[Vine#Twining_vines|twining vine]] (bine) is very [[hardiness (plants)|hardy]] (hence the name hardy kiwi), and is capable of surviving slow temperature drops to {{cvt|−45|°C}}, and summer temperatures exceeding {{cvt|37|°C}},{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|p=42}} although young shoots can be vulnerable to frost in the spring.[http://ssfruit.cas.psu.edu/HardyKiwi.htm Hardy Kiwi] Hardy Kiwi. Dec. 16, 2008, Penn State College of Agricultural Sciences. The vines need a frost-free growing season of about 150 days, but are not damaged by late freezes, provided that temperature changes are sufficiently gradual to allow plants to acclimate. Indeed, a period of winter chill is necessary for successful cultivation. However, rapid freezes kill off buds and split vines. The vines can also be grown in low-chill areas. While hardy kiwi may be grown directly from seeds (germination time is about one month), propagating from [[Cutting (plant)|cuttings]] is also possible. Growing from seeds needs a period of cold stratification of one to two months to germinate. Hardy kiwi cuttings may be [[grafted]] directly onto established kiwifruit [[rootstock]], or [[root]]ed themselves. In domestic cultivation, a [[Trellis|trellis]] may be used to encourage horizontal growth for easy maintenance and harvesting; however, vines grow extremely quickly and require a strong trellis for support. Each vine can grow up to {{cvt|20|ft}} in a single season, given ideal growing conditions.[http://www.garden.org/articles/articles.php?q=show&id=656&page=1 Hardy Kiwi] Nan Sterman, National Gardening Association. For commercial planting, placement is important: plants can tolerate partial shade, but yields are optimized with full sunlight. Hardy kiwi vines consume large volumes of water; therefore, they are usually grown in well-drained, acidic soils to prevent root rot. === Pollination and harvest === For vines to bear fruit, both male and female plants must be present to enable pollination. A male pollinator can enable six female producers to fruit. Flowering typically occurs in late spring (May in the Northern Hemisphere) starting in the third year of growth.{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20121215022750/http://ohioline.osu.edu/hyg-fact/1000/1426.html|title=Kiwifruit and Hardy Kiwi}} Kiwifruit and Hardy Kiwi HYG-1426-93. John Strang & Richard C. Funt, Ohio State University. If flowers become frost-burned, however, no fruit production will occur during the remainder of the year. An autumn harvest is standard among all varieties; within this, actual harvest times are highly dependent on local climate and the specific cultivar grown. Each individual female vine can produce up to 100 pounds of fruit per year, but average annual yield is roughly 50 lb per vine. Both fruit size and total yield are highly cultivar-dependent. Fruit left to ripen on the vine has an 18 to 25% sugar content at time of harvest. Some hardy kiwifruit varieties may benefit from harvesting after a frost, a form of [[bletting]].{{Cite journal |last=Kataoka |first=I. |last2=Ono |first2=K. |last3=Beppu |first3=K. |date=June 2025 |title=Potential of Actinidia arguta var. hypoleuca endemic to Japan for utilization as a kiwiberry |url=https://www.actahort.org/books/1431/1431_27.htm |journal=Acta Horticulturae |issue=1431 |pages=209–216 |doi=10.17660/ActaHortic.2025.1431.27 |issn=0567-7572|url-access=subscription }} === Pests === Hardy kiwi vines are vulnerable to several botanical diseases, including [[phytophthora]] crown and root rot (the most serious problem), [[Botryotinia|botrytis]] rot, and [[sclerotinia]] [[blight]]. Vines are also vulnerable to pest infestations, including root knot [[nematodes]], [[two-spotted spider mites]], [[leaf rollers]], [[thrips]], and [[Japanese beetles]]. Cats can also pose a problem, as they are attracted to a [[catnip]]-like smell produced by the hardy kiwi vines. Cats have been known to destroy vines and dig up roots in search of the source of the scent. == Culinary use == {{Nutritionalvalue | name = Hardy kiwifruit, fresh, raw | image = Actinidia-arguta.jpg | caption = Cross-sectioned and whole
hardy kiwifruit (''Actinidia arguta'') | kJ= 322 | protein= 1.2 g | fat= 0.6 g | carbs= 18 g | fiber= 3 g | sugars= 7.6 g | potassium_mg=288 | sodium_mg= 6 | vitC_mg= 93 | source=[http://nzkiwiberry.com/about_nutrition.html NZ KiwiBerry Growers Inc.
Nutritional Value] }} Kiwiberries are primarily produced for the fresh fruit market, sold in small punnets as a ready-to-eat fruit.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|p=129}} Kiwiberries are also processed into jams, preserved fruit and juices.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|p=130}}{{Cite web |title=다래 |url=https://www.doopedia.co.kr/mo/doopedia/master/master.do?_method=view2&MAS_IDX=101013000731533 |access-date=2025-05-03 |website=www.doopedia.co.kr |language=ko}} In China, kiwiberry food additives such as nutritional powders and fruit vinegars are commercially available, and kiwiberry wines are produced in the United States.{{sfn|Latocha|Debersaques|Hale|2021|p=130}} In [[Korean cuisine|Korea]], kiwiberries are known as ''darae'' ({{lang|ko|다래}}). Young leaves, called ''darae-sun'', are often consumed as ''[[namul]]'' vegetable.{{cite news|last1=Kwon|first1=Daeik|title=Saenggimsae biseutan bomnamul sigyong – dokcho chakgak swiwo|url=http://www.hankookilbo.com/v/95c921717b3242c69ef959da195a7979|accessdate=27 December 2017|work=[[Hankook Ilbo]]|language=ko}} The vines can be tapped in early spring to gather [[sap]],{{Cite web |last=쿠키뉴스 |date=2025-02-18 |title=바뀌는 과수 재배 지도…'토종 다래' 주목 |url=https://www.kukinews.com/article/view/kuk202502180080#_enliple |access-date=2025-05-03 |website=쿠키뉴스 |language=ko}} which migratory farmers in [[Gangwon Province, South Korea|Gangwon province]] are said to have used as a food source during famines.{{Cite web |last=인터넷신문 |first=전북일보 |date=2002-07-19 |title=[남원] 다래나무 수액 음용수로 개발 |url=https://www.jjan.kr/article/20020718067042 |access-date=2025-05-03 |website=전북일보 인터넷신문 |language=ko}} === Gallery === File:Kiwibesstroop Hoogstraten open.JPG|Kiwiberry [[jam]] Dried hardy kiwi shoots.jpg|Dried young leaves, sold as ''[[namul]]'' vegetable Міні-ківі.png|Kiwiberry punnet sold in Ukraine == See also == * [[Actinidia chinensis var. deliciosa|''Actinidia chinensis'' var.
